## [v8.0.0-rc.2](https://github.com/prisma/prisma/releases/tag/v8.0.0-rc.2)
*GitHub Releases · Prisma 7* | 17/08/2026 | Score: 1.00
Tags: api_update, developer_tool, cli_tool, tool_update

> <h1>v8.0.0-rc.2</h1> <p>This release retires the <code>prisma-next</code> binary in favour of the unified <code>prisma</code> CLI, returns the default aggregates to plain JavaScript numbers with lossless variants beside them, makes CHECK constraints a declared part of the contract, and splits runtime row queries from non-returning writes. Almost every application will need to re-emit its contract and rename its config file, so read the breaking changes before upgrading.</p> <p>Two upgrade recipes carry the mechanical translations for this hop: the <a href="https://github.com/prisma/prisma/blob/v8.0.0-rc.2/skills/prisma-next-upgrade/upgrades/8.0.0-rc.1-to-8.0.0-rc.2/">user recipe</a> and the <a href="https://github.com/prisma/prisma/blob/v8.0.0-rc.2/skills/prisma-8-extension-upgrade/upgrades/8.0.0-rc.1-to-8.0.0-rc.2/">extension-author recipe</a>.</p> <h2>Breaking changes</h2> <ul> <li> <p><strong>This repository no longer publishes a CLI; the unified <code>prisma</code> CLI replaces it</strong> — nothing published ships a <code>prisma-next</code> bin anymore. <code>@prisma/orm-toolchain</code> exposes the <code>orm</code> command family at <code>@prisma/orm-toolchain/cli</code> and no binary, and the database facades forward no launcher. Install <code>@prisma/cli</code> (the prisma-cli distribution, published under <code>next</code> for the v8 line) and replace <code>prisma-next <command></code> in package scripts and CI with the unified CLI. The config file moves with it: <code>prisma-next.config.ts</code> is deprecated in favour of <code>prisma.config.ts</code>, and the config value is now engine-shaped, with your existing ORM config nested under an <code>orm</code> section. Both the old filename and the flat shape still load, each printing a deprecation warning on stderr, so the rename and the rewrap can land separately. See the <a href="https://github.com/prisma/prisma/blob/v8.0.0-rc.2/skills/prisma-next-upgrade/upgrades/8.0.0-rc.1-to-8.0.0-rc.2/">user recipe</a>. (<a href="https://github.com/prisma/prisma/pull/30005" data-hovercard-type="pull_request" data-hovercard-url="/prisma/prisma/pull/30005/hovercard">#30005</a>)</p> <p>Before:</p> <div class="highlight highlight-source-ts notranslate position-relative overflow-auto" data-snippet-clipboard-copy-content="// prisma-next.config.ts import { defineConfig } from '@prisma/orm-postgres/config'; export default defineConfig({ contract: './contract.ts', output: './generated' });"><pre><span class="pl-c">// prisma-next.config.ts</span> <span class="pl-k">import</span> <span class="pl-kos">{</span> <span class="pl-s1">defineConfig</span> <span class="pl-kos">}</span> <span class="pl-k">from</span> <span class="pl-s">'@prisma/orm-postgres/config'</span><span class="pl-kos">;</span> <span class="pl-k">export</span> <span class="pl-k">default</span> <span class="pl-en">defineConfig</span><span class="pl-kos">(</span><span class="pl-kos">{</span> <span class="pl-c1">contract</span>: <span class="pl-s">'./contract.ts'</span><span class="pl-kos">,</span> <span class="pl-c1">output</span>: <span class="pl-s">'./generated'</span> <span class="pl-kos">}</span><span class="pl-kos">)</span><span class="pl-kos">;</span></pre></div> <p>After:</p> <div class="highlight highlight-source-ts notranslate position-relative overflow-auto" data-snippet-clipboard-copy-content="// prisma.config.ts import { defineConfig } from '@prisma/cli-engine'; import { defineConfig as ormConfig } from '@prisma/orm-postgres/config'; export default defineConfig({ orm: ormConfig({ contract: './contract.ts', output: './generated' }), });"><pre><span class="pl-c">// prisma.config.ts</span> <span class="pl-k">import</span> <span class="pl-kos">{</span> <span class="pl-s1">defineConfig</span> <span class="pl-kos">}</span> <span class="pl-k">from</span> <span class="pl-s">'@prisma/cli-engine'</span><span class="pl-kos">;</span> <span class="pl-k">import</span> <span class="pl-kos">{</span> <span class="pl-s1">defineConfig</span> <span class="pl-k">as</span> <span class="pl-s1">ormConfig</span> <span class="pl-kos">}</span> <span class="pl-k">from</span> <span class="pl-s">'@prisma/orm-postgres/config'</span><span class="pl-kos">;</span> <span class="pl-k">export</span> <span class="pl-k">default</span> <span class="pl-en">defineConfig</span><span class="pl-kos">(</span><span class="pl-kos">{</span> <span class="pl-c1">orm</span>: <span class="pl-en">ormConfig</span><span class="pl-kos">(</span><span class="pl-kos">{</span> <span class="pl-c1">contract</span>: <span class="pl-s">'./contract.ts'</span><span class="pl-kos">,</span> <span class="pl-c1">output</span>: <span class="pl-s">'./generated'</span> <span class="pl-kos">}</span><span class="pl-kos">)</span><span class="pl-kos">,</span> <span class="pl-kos">}</span><span class="pl-kos">)</span><span class="pl-kos">;</span></pre></div> </li> <li> <p><strong>The default aggregates are JavaScript numbers again, with lossless variants beside them</strong> — <code>count()</code>, <code>sum()</code> over an integer column, and <code>avg()</code> over an integer column all return <code>number</code>. In <code>8.0.0-rc.1</code> they returned a <code>bigint</code>, a <code>bigint</code> or decimal string depending on the column's width, and a decimal string respectively. The lossless results moved to three new operations: <code>countBigInt()</code> returns a <code>bigint</code>, <code>sumBigInt()</code> returns a <code>bigint</code>, and <code>avgDecimal()</code> returns an exact decimal string (PostgreSQL only — SQLite has no decimal type and contributes none). A <code>count()</code> or integer <code>sum()</code> whose value passes ±(2^53 − 1) now raises <code>RUNTIME.DECODE_FAILED</code> rather than returning a rounded number, so move those calls to the <code>BigInt</code> variants where the magnitude is real. Unchanged: <code>min</code>/<code>max</code>, <code>sum</code>/<code>avg</code> over a float column, <code>sum</code> over <code>Decimal</code>, <code>sum</code> over <code>UnboundedInt</code>, and the ORM's <code>having(...)</code> operands. The SQL builder's comparison operands do move, because <code>fns.gt(a, b)</code> types both sides from one codec. The same PR also makes the wide-integer codecs refuse the wrong JavaScript type: a <code>BigInt</code> or <code>UnboundedInt</code> column rejects a <code>number</code> and a <code>BigIntNumber</code> column rejects a <code>bigint</code>, with <code>RUNTIME.ENCODE_FAILED</code> naming the type that arrived, where previously a number was accepted and stringified — which let a fractional value reach an integer column unremarked. See the <a href="https://github.com/prisma/prisma/blob/v8.0.0-rc.2/skills/prisma-next-upgrade/upgrades/8.0.0-rc.1-to-8.0.0-rc.2/">user recipe</a>. (<a href="https://github.com/prisma/prisma/pull/29930" data-hovercard-type="pull_request" data-hovercard-url="/prisma/prisma/pull/29930/hovercard">#29930</a>)</p> <p>Before:</p> <div class="highlight highlight-source-ts notranslate position-relative overflow-auto" data-snippet-clipboard-copy-content="const { total } = await db.User.aggregate((a) => ({ total: a.count() })); total === 2n; // bigint const busy = await db.sql.public.user .groupBy('kind') .having((_f, fns) => fns.gt(fns.count(), 1n)); // bigint literal"><pre><span class="pl-k">const</span> <span class="pl-kos">{</span> total <span class="pl-kos">}</span> <span class="pl-c1">=</span> <span class="pl-k">await</span> <span class="pl-s1">db</span><span class="pl-kos">.</span><span class="pl-c1">User</span><span class="pl-kos">.</span><span class="pl-en">aggregate</span><span class="pl-kos">(</span><span class="pl-kos">(</span><span class="pl-s1">a</span><span class="pl-kos">)</span> <span class="pl-c1">=></span> <span class="pl-kos">(</span><span class="pl-kos">{</span> <span class="pl-c1">total</span>: <span class="pl-s1">a</span><span class="pl-kos">.</span><span aggregate methods exist is now the contract's answer</strong> — the aggregate methods are no longer declared on the ORM and SQL-builder surfaces outright. Each surface is derived from the operation names in the emitted <code>contract.d.ts</code>'s <code>AggregateTypes</code> block, so a target or extension can contribute an operation and it appears under its own name with no client change. PostgreSQL now contributes eight operations and SQLite seven. <strong>Re-emit your contract</strong> with the CLI's <code>contract emit</code>: against a contract with no <code>AggregateTypes</code> block — one authored in code with <code>defineContract(...)</code> and handed straight to the client, or emitted before <code>8.0.0-rc.1</code> — every aggregate surface resolves to <code>AggregateOperationsUnavailable</code>, an empty type, and each call becomes a compile error. What this release changes is compile-time only — the separate runtime guard introduced in <code>8.0.0-rc.1</code> still stands, rejecting an aggregate whose operation and input codec the composed target does not declare with <code>ORM.AGGREGATE_UNSUPPORTED</code> before the query runs. Separately, <code>count(field)</code> now renders <code>COUNT(<column>)</code> instead of accepting the argument and discarding it, so a call that got past the types — a <code>@ts-expect-error</code>, a <code>count(x as never)</code>, or dynamic dispatch — now counts that field's non-null values rather than rows. See the <a href="https://github.com/prisma/prisma/blob/v8.0.0-rc.2/skills/prisma-next-upgrade/upgrades/8.0.0-rc.1-to-8.0.0-rc.2/">user recipe</a> and the <a href="https://github.com/prisma/prisma/blob/v8.0.0-rc.2/skills/prisma-8-extension-upgrade/upgrades/8.0.0-rc.1-to-8.0.0-rc.2/">extension-author recipe</a>. (<a href="https://github.com/prisma/prisma/pull/29922" data-hovercard-type="pull_request" data-hovercard-url="/prisma/prisma/pull/29922/hovercard">#29922</a>)</p> </li> <li> <p><strong>CHECK constraints are declared in the contract, and introspection now sees all of them</strong> — the CHECK shape in <code>contract.json</code> changed from <code>{ name, column, valueSet }</code> to <code>{ name, prefix, expression }</code>, where <code>expression</code> is the raw SQL predicate and <code>name</code> is a content-addressed wire name (<code><prefix>_<8hex></code>, the convention indexes and RLS policies already use). An old-shape contract is rejected on read, so re-emitting is not optional. Three consequences to plan for. Your first migration plan after upgrading drops each old unsuffixed enum constraint and adds the wire-named one, which needs <code>destructive</code> to converge. Every list (<code>many</code>) column gains a declared element-non-null CHECK the planner previously created without declaring. And introspection stopped parsing predicates, so hand-written constraints earlier versions could not see are now visible — and an undeclared check is an extra that <code>db verify --strict</code> reports and a destructive-capable plan drops, so read the first plan for <code>dropCheckConstraint</code> operations naming constraints you wrote yourself, and declare each one you want to keep with <code>@@check(expression: "…", map: "<physical name>")</code>. Two API changes ride along: <code>addCheckConstraint</code> in committed migration files takes an <code>expression</code> instead of a <code>column</code>/<code>values</code> pair, and the <code>typescriptContract</code> options bag now requires <code>createNamespace</code> whenever it passes <code>defaultControlPolicy</code>. An <code>enumType()</code> whose codec is numeric now throws <code>CONTRACT.ENUM_INVALID</code> while the contract is being built rather than failing later at migrate time. See the <a href="https://github.com/prisma/prisma/blob/v8.0.0-rc.2/skills/prisma-next-upgrade/upgrades/8.0.0-rc.1-to-8.0.0-rc.2/">user recipe</a> and the <a href="https://github.com/prisma/prisma/blob/v8.0.0-rc.2/skills/prisma-8-extension-upgrade/upgrades/8.0.0-rc.1-to-8.0.0-rc.2/">extension-author recipe</a>. (<a href="https://github.com/prisma/prisma/pull/29892" data-hovercard-type="pull_request" data-hovercard-url="/prisma/prisma/pull/29892/hovercard">#29892</a>)</p> <p>Before:</p> <div class="highlight class="pl-kos">;</span></pre></div> </li> <li> <p><strong>Runtime row queries and non-returning writes are separate calls</strong> — <code>query()</code> streams rows and <code>execute()</code> resolves <code>{ affectedRows }</code>, which is how a write now reports its affected count without a preceding <code>SELECT</code>. Classify each call site by the result it consumes rather than replacing every <code>execute</code>: a select, a returning write, or any plan whose rows are iterated, indexed, or decoded moves to <code>query</code>, while an insert, update, or delete that returns nothing stays on <code>execute</code> and reads <code>affectedRows</code>. Prepared row consumption moves from <code>target.queryPrepared(prepared, params)</code> to <code>prepared.query(target, params)</code>. Runtime middleware splits the same way, into <code>beforeQuery</code> / <code>interceptQuery</code> / <code>afterQuery</code> and <code>beforeExecute</code> / <code>interceptExecute</code> / <code>afterExecute</code> with a shared <code>beforeCompile</code>; query interception returns <code>{ rows }</code> and execute interception returns <code>{ stats }</code>. There is no operation discriminator, compatibility alias, or generic fallback hook. On Mongo, <code>db.query</code> stays the static builder and the row-executing <code>db.execute</code> facade method is gone — build with <code>db.query</code>, then execute through <code>(await db.runtime()).query(plan)</code>. See the <a href="https://github.com/prisma/prisma/blob/v8.0.0-rc.2/skills/prisma-next-upgrade/upgrades/8.0.0-rc.1-to-8.0.0-rc.2/">user recipe</a>. (<a href="https://github.com/prisma/prisma/pull/29921" data-hovercard-type="pull_request" data-hovercard-url="/prisma/prisma/pull/29921/hovercard">#29921</a>)</p> </li> <li> <p><strong><code>raw</code> is a reserved storage namespace</strong> — the SQL surface exposes the whole-query raw statement tag as <code>db.sql.raw</code>, so a storage namespace of that name would be unreachable through the builder while the emitted types still promised its tables. Building the client now raises <code>ORM.NAMESPACE_RESERVED</code> naming the namespace. Rename it in your schema, re-emit the contract, and plan the rename against the database as you would any other namespace rename. Only <code>raw</code> is reserved. (<a href="https://github.com/prisma/prisma/pull/29997" data-hovercard-type="pull_request" data-hovercard-url="/prisma/prisma/pull/29997/hovercard">#29997</a>)</p> <p>Before:</p> <div class="highlight highlight-source-prisma notranslate position-relative overflow-auto" data-snippet-clipboard-copy-content="model Event { id String @id @@schema("raw") }"><pre><span class="pl-s1"><span class="pl-k">model</span> <span class="pl-en">Event</span> {</span> <span class="pl-s1"> <span class="pl-smi">id</span> <span class="pl-c1">String</span> <span class="pl-s1"><span class="pl-en">@id</span></span></span> <span class="pl-s1"> <span class="pl-s1"><span class="pl-en">@@schema</span>(<span class="pl-s">"</span><span class="pl-s">raw</span><span class="pl-s">"</span>)</span></span> <span class="pl-s1">}</span></pre></div> <p>After:</p> <div class="highlight highlight-source-prisma notranslate position-relative overflow-auto" data-snippet-clipboard-copy-content="model Event { id String @id @@schema("ingest") }"><pre><span class="pl-s1"><span class="pl-k">model</span> <span class="pl-en">Event</span> {</span> <span class="pl-s1"> <span class="pl-smi">id</span> <span class="pl-c1">String</span> <span class="pl-s1"><span class="pl-en">@id</span></span></span> <span class="pl-s1"> <span class="pl-s1"><span class="pl-en">@@schema</span>(<span class="pl-s">"</span><span class="pl-s">ingest</span><span class="pl-s">"</span>)</span></span> <span class="pl-s1">}</span></pre></div> </li> <li> <p><strong>Codec ids are checked where you write them</strong> — a codec id in a prepared declaration or in a contract-bound raw fragment is now checked against your contract's codec map, so an id the contract does not carry is a compile error instead of an execution-time <code>RUNTIME.PARAM_REF_MISSING_CODEC</code>. The usual cause is an unversioned id. Read the correct spelling off your emitted <code>contract.d.ts</code> — every id it carries now completes at both positions. A raw fragment built through a contract-free lane is unaffected, since it has no map to check against. the CLI style guide has always said a blanket confirmation flag must not stand in for a destructive confirmation. Non-interactive runs grant with <code>--confirm <database></code>. A dry run, or a plan with nothing destructive in it, never asks. Update any CI invocation that relied on <code>-y</code> to apply a destructive plan. (<a href="https://github.com/prisma/prisma/pull/29986" data-hovercard-type="pull_request" data-hovercard-url="/prisma/prisma/pull/29986/hovercard">#29986</a>)</p> </li> <li> <p><strong>The diagnostic commands exit 4 on findings and 2 on errors</strong> — <code>db verify</code>, <code>db sign</code>, and <code>migration check</code> now distinguish "I ran and found problems" (exit 4) from "I could not run" (exit 2). Exit 1 is reserved for a bug in the CLI itself, and exit 0 still means the check ran and found nothing. <code>db verify</code> and <code>db sign</code> previously exited 1 on findings, and <code>migration check</code> exited 2. Scripts that test for any non-zero exit are unaffected; scripts that match a specific code must be updated. (<a href="https://github.com/prisma/prisma/pull/29984" data-hovercard-type="pull_request" data-hovercard-url="/prisma/prisma/pull/29984/hovercard">#29984</a>)</p> </li> <li> <p><strong>Four <code>migration status</code> flags are retired</strong> — <code>--graph</code>, <code>--all</code>, <code>--limit</code>, and <code>--ref</code> moved to their own commands. An old invocation now gets a typed <code>CLI.COMMAND_MOVED</code> error naming the replacement rather than failing as an unknown flag. (<a href="https://github.com/prisma/prisma/pull/29982" data-hovercard-type="pull_request" data-hovercard-url="/prisma/prisma/pull/29982/hovercard">#29982</a>)</p> </li> <li> <p><strong>Prepared statements split by their declared result</strong> — <code>runtime.prepare()</code> returns one of two handles chosen from the plan the callback builds: a rows plan gives the <code>PreparedStatement</code> you already have, consumed with <code>.query(target, params)</code>, while a plan whose declared result is an affected-row count gives a <code>PreparedExecution</code>, consumed with <code>.execute(target, params)</code>. This matters to extension authors: a facade that redeclares <code>prepare()</code> changes its return type to <code>PreparedFor</code> with no logic change, and a scope that installs the prepared-query bridge must also install the execute bridge or <code>prepared.execute</code> throws on the bridge invariant. See the <a href="https://github.com/prisma/prisma/blob/v8.0.0-rc.2/skills/prisma-8-extension-upgrade/upgrades/8.0.0-rc.1-to-8.0.0-rc.2/">extension-author recipe</a>. (<a href="https://github.com/prisma/prisma/pull/30006" data-hovercard-type="pull_request" data-hovercard-url="/prisma/prisma/pull/30006/hovercard">#30006</a>)</p> </li> </ul> <h2>Features</h2> <ul> <li>Whole-query raw SQL replaces the classic <code>$queryRaw</code> / <code>$executeRaw</code> use case. A whole statement is authored with the same tagged template the fragment mechanism already used, terminated with <code>.returnsRow(rowSpec)</code> for decoded, typed rows or <code>.affectedCount()</code> for a mutation count, and built into an ordinary query plan that flows through the existing lowering, codec, guardrail, and execution machinery — no new query lane and no new execution surface. Row-returning raw queries interpolate into other raw templates as subqueries, which gives CTEs, including data-modifying ones, for free. (<a href="https://github.com/prisma/prisma/pull/29997" data-hovercard-type="pull_request" data-hovercard-url="/prisma/prisma/pull/29997/hovercard">#29997</a>)</li> <li><code>@@check(expression: "…")</code> declares a CHECK constraint in the schema, and <code>contract infer</code> adopts the ones your database already has. Use <code>name:</code> for a wire-name prefix, so the physical constraint is <code>name_<8hex></code> hashed over the predicate and compared by name — which means Postgres reprinting the expression never causes drift. Use <code>map:</code> to adopt a constraint under its existing physical name, comparing the predicate byte-for-byte. Pulling a database now emits <code>@@check</code> for every live check Prisma Next did not derive, so a hand-written constraint is declared from the first pull instead of reading as an undeclared extra. (<a href="https://github.com/prisma/prisma/pull/29972" data-hovercard-type="pull_request" data-hovercard-url="/prisma/prisma/pull/29972/hovercard">#29972</a>)</li> <li><code>@noCheck</code> opts a column out of the CHECK constraints Prisma Next derives for it, per kind: <code>@noCheck</code> suppresses all of them, <code>@noCheck(membership)</code> keeps the element-non-null check on a list column while dropping the membership check, and <code>@noCheck(elementNotNull)</code> does the reverse. The TypeScript builder equivalent is <code>.noCheck(...)</code>. <code>contract infer</code> emits the attribute too, so a pulled schema passes <code>db verify --schema-only</code> immediately instead of needing one migration first. (<a href="https://github.com/prisma/prisma/pull/29928" data-hovercard-type="pull_request" data-hovercard-url="/prisma/prisma/pull/29928/hovercard">#29928</a>)</li> <li>Two new column types make integer representation a per-column choice without changing the lossless <code>BigInt</code> default. <code>BigIntNumber</code> reads and writes as a JavaScript <code>number</code>, throwing outside ±(2^53 − 1) instead of rounding. <code>UnboundedInt</code> uses PostgreSQL unconstrained <code>numeric</code> storage and round-trips integral values as exact <code>bigint</code> values at arbitrary magnitude. PostgreSQL contributes both; SQLite contributes <code>BigIntNumber</code>. (<a href="https://github.com/prisma/prisma/pull/29902" data-hovercard-type="pull_request" data-hovercard-url="/prisma/prisma/pull/29902/hovercard">#29902</a>)</li> <li>The minimum supported PostgreSQL version drops from 17 to 15, the oldest version CI has been exercising all along. <code>init</code> scaffolds and the <code>--probe-db</code> warning threshold follow the new floor. The reasoning is recorded in ADR 244. (<a href="https://github.com/prisma/prisma/pull/29971" data-hovercard-type="pull_request" data-hovercard-url="/prisma/prisma/pull/29971/hovercard">#29971</a>)</li> <li>Renaming a model or column whose CHECK constraint content is unchanged now plans a single <code>ALTER TABLE … RENAME CONSTRAINT</code>, classed <code>widening</code>, instead of a drop plus an add. A cosmetic rename no longer needs a destructive-capable plan or a full table revalidation. (<a href="https://github.com/prisma/prisma/pull/29894" data-hovercard-type="pull_request" data-hovercard-url="/prisma/prisma/pull/29894/hovercard">#29894</a>)</li> <li>Errors carry typed next actions. A failure that has a remedy now ships it as structured data — <code>nextActions</code>, each naming a command to run — raised at the site that holds the arguments rather than spelled out in English prose a caller would have to parse. The binary name is templated at the raise site and substituted when rendered, so the suggestion stays correct as the CLI is renamed. (<a href="https://github.com/prisma/prisma/pull/29977" data-hovercard-type="pull_request" data-hovercard-url="/prisma/prisma/pull/29977/hovercard">#29977</a>)</li> <li>CLI failures report their real error code. <code>envelope.code</code> is the stable surface consumers branch on, and a dozen failures previously reported <code>CONTRACT.VERIFY_FAILED</code> while hiding the true code in metadata. Every construction site now declares its code explicitly, fourteen new codes were added for the failures that had none, and the generic error path gained <code>cause</code> support. (<a href="https://github.com/prisma/prisma/pull/29919" data-hovercard-type="pull_request" data-hovercard-url="/prisma/prisma/pull/29919/hovercard">#29919</a>)</li> <li>Config loading reports diagnostics per section instead of throwing on the first problem it finds. A command fails only when a section it actually reads is broken, so a malformed <code>formatter</code> section no longer blocks <code>db init</code>. Each diagnostic is tagged with the config section and field it concerns. (<a href="https://github.com/prisma/prisma/pull/29936" data-hovercard-type="pull_request" data-hovercard-url="/prisma/prisma/pull/29936/hovercard">#29936</a>)</li> </ul> <h2>Fixes</h2> <ul> <li><code>init</code> no longer fails at its contract-emit step against the published packages. The step now runs the scaffolded project's own CLI binary as a subprocess rather than loading the new config in-process with the running CLI's bundled loader, and its failure message carries the child's stderr so a real cause is visible. The schema-path prompt also shows its default as placeholder text instead of looking blank until a keypress. (<a href="https://github.com/prisma/prisma/pull/30018" data-hovercard-type="pull_request" data-hovercard-url="/prisma/prisma/pull/30018/hovercard">#30018</a>)</li> <li><code>contract emit</code> picks the import specifier for the emitted <code>contract.d.ts</code> by reading the nearest <code>package.json</code> above the file it is writing, rather than falling back to the process working directory. Running the command from the wrong directory previously wrote an unresolvable internal specifier into the generated file. (<a href="https://github.com/prisma/prisma/pull/29981" data-hovercard-type="pull_request" data-hovercard-url="/prisma/prisma/pull/29981/hovercard">#29981</a>)</li> <li>Synthesized foreign-key-backing index name prefixes are truncated to fit PostgreSQL's 63-byte identifier limit, so a mapped explicit join table no longer fails <code>contract emit</code> before the content hash can be appended. User-authored over-budget index prefixes still fail loudly. (<a href="https://github.com/prisma/prisma/pull/30025" data-hovercard-type="pull_request" data-hovercard-url="/prisma/prisma/pull/30025/hovercard">#30025</a>)</li> <li>A raw row spec column named <code>__proto__</code> is now refused loudly instead of silently vanishing — bracket assignment onto an object literal hit the inherited setter, so the key never became an own property and the record was quietly re-parented. <code>constructor</code> and <code>prototype</code> create ordinary own properties and round-trip faithfully. (<a href="https://github.com/prisma/prisma/pull/30014" data-hovercard-type="pull_request" data-hovercard-url="/prisma/prisma/pull/30014/hovercard">#30014</a>)</li> <li>The PostgreSQL direct driver no longer ends a caller's transaction. A driver-level read issued while its connection held an open transaction reported no transaction in progress, took the cursor portal-protection path, and wrapped itself in <code>BEGIN</code>/<code>COMMIT</code> — and that <code>COMMIT</code> ended the caller's transaction, so later statements ran autocommit and <code>ROLLBACK</code> undid nothing. The driver and its connection now share the transaction-open flag. (<a href="https://github.com/prisma/prisma/pull/29920" data-hovercard-type="pull_request" data-hovercard-url="/prisma/prisma/pull/29920/hovercard">#29920</a>)</li> <li>ORM mutation reloads encode <code>Bytes</code> identities through the column codec, so a repeated upsert keyed on a <code>Bytes</code> column no longer raises <code>ORM.MUTATION_ROW_MISSING</code>. Every unbound literal entering a select through raw collection state now becomes a typed parameter. (<a href="https://github.com/prisma/prisma/pull/29910" data-hovercard-type="pull_request" data-hovercard-url="/prisma/prisma/pull/29910/hovercard">#29910</a>)</li> </ul> <h2>New contributors</h2> <ul> <li><a href="https://github.com/EmaToplek">@EmaToplek</a> made their first contribution in <a href="https://github.com/prisma/prisma/pull/29903" data-hovercard-type="pull_request" data-hovercard-url="/prisma/prisma/pull/29903/hovercard">#29903</a></li> </ul>

## [Chris Carter is mistaken if he thinks more gore will bring The X-Files: I Want to Believe back to life](https://www.theguardian.com/film/2026/aug/17/chris-carter-x-files-i-want-to-believe-directors-cut-critique-spoilers)
*The Guardian (Culture)* | 17/08/2026 | Score: 0.86
Tags: github_release, tool_update

> <p>The director’s cut includes a host more body parts but no more insight into the villains’ personalities. What could be a gothic masterstroke is turned into a dreary procedural in the snow</p><p><strong>Warning: this article contains spoilers</strong></p><p>Everyone loves a director’s cut. But unlike some, The X-Files: I Want to Believe – Vrach Frankenshteyn, which debuted on Friday on Disney+, is not the kind of director’s cut that will radically alter critical perspectives on <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/film/2008/aug/01/sciencefictionandfantasy1">the original 2008 film</a>. Much has been made, <a href="https://ew.com/see-trailer-chris-carter-scarier-r-rated-director-cut-the-x-files-i-want-to-believe-12031493">mainly by director and X-Files creator Chris Carter</a>, of the new version’s grisly additions. But there is still so much about this movie that is underwritten, preposterous and lacking in basic dramatic intrigue that upping its body horror quotient merely makes the same old problems slightly more unpleasant to look at. Perhaps unsurprisingly, this new version is hidden away behind the “Extras” tab for the original film.</p><p>For those who have sensibly forgotten, I Want to Believe reunites Mulder (David Duchovny) and Scully (Gillian Anderson) several years after their departure from the FBI, when a female agent disappears and the bureau’s only lead comes from a disgraced former Catholic priest (Billy Connolly) who claims to be receiving psychic visions. So far, so X-Files. The priest, Father Joe, is a convicted paedophile who abused dozens of altar boys, which gives Scully some fairly understandable reservations about accepting his apparent supernatural gifts at face value.</p> <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/film/2026/aug/17/chris-carter-x-files-i-want-to-believe-directors-cut-critique-spoilers">Continue reading...</a>
